column5: God knows a word before it reaches the tongue
column6: The commentary says the one who eases the prophet knows what is hidden within him. The psalm says God knows the speaker's word before it is on his tongue, joining inward knowledge to speech before utterance.

column5: God's Spirit causes the people to walk in the statutes
column6: The commentary's central distinction is that the traveler is made ready, not merely given a smoother road. Ezekiel promises God's Spirit within the people will cause them to walk in God's statutes, directly locating readiness in the walkers.

column5: A voice commands that the Lord's way be prepared
column6: The commentary stresses that the ayah makes the person easy while the road remains. Isaiah instead commands preparation of the Lord's way in the wilderness, a precise contrast in what is readied.

column5: Valleys are raised and rough ground made level
column6: The commentary says ease can be placed in the traveler's gait even when the route is difficult. Isaiah pictures the route itself being leveled, so the shared journey image makes the different means of easing clear.

column5: Luke applies Isaiah's prepared-way voice to John
column6: The commentary contrasts preparing the traveler with smoothing the path. Luke quotes Isaiah's command to prepare the Lord's way as the setting for John the Baptist's preaching, making the voice of a prophet the means of preparing a route.

column5: Wisdom's instruction keeps the walk and run unhindered
column6: The commentary says the messenger is made light-footed and ready for the way. Proverbs says the instructed person's step will not be hampered when walking or stumbling when running, linking guidance with unhindered movement.

column5: God gives the speaker a deer's feet for the heights
column6: The commentary develops the image of a responsive mount with light legs that carries its rider over a route. The psalm says God makes the speaker's feet like a deer's and sets him on the heights, a close image of divinely enabled movement.

column5: God widens the space beneath the speaker's steps
column6: The commentary says the road stays as it is while the traveler is made ready. The psalm credits God with widening the speaker's steps so his feet do not slip, bringing the contrasting image of the route itself made spacious.

column5: God gives deer-like feet on high places amid scarcity
column6: The commentary's light-footed traveler can keep moving even when the route is steep. Habakkuk says God makes his feet like a deer's and enables him to tread on heights, in a passage that names famine and crop failure immediately before this trust.

column5: The messenger's feet carry news of peace and salvation
column6: The commentary brings together the prophet's reminder and the image of light steps on a route. Isaiah praises the feet of the messenger who announces peace and salvation, joining movement to the work of proclamation.

column5: Paul applies Isaiah's beautiful feet to gospel proclamation
column6: The commentary's prepared messenger is enabled to carry a reminder. Paul quotes Isaiah's messenger with beautiful feet to explain the sending of Christian preachers, giving the older restoration image an apostolic preaching interpretation.

column5: God equips the community to do God's will
column6: The commentary reads ease as preparation of the person for continuing work. Hebrews asks God to equip the community with everything good for doing God's will and to work within them, a direct Christian formulation of inwardly enabled service.

column5: A cleansed vessel is prepared for every good work
column6: The commentary hears “we will make you easy” as “we will prepare you” for the assigned task. Second Timothy describes a person as a vessel prepared for every good work, giving that secondary sense a concrete Christian counterpart.

column5: The good works are prepared for the believer to walk in
column6: The commentary emphasizes that the prophet himself is the direct object of preparation. Ephesians says God prepared the good works beforehand for believers to walk in, shifting preparation from the person to the course of action.

column5: The Lord who knows hearts is asked to choose a messenger
column6: The commentary connects the promise of ease with the speaker's knowledge of what is hidden in a person. Before a lot selects an apostle, Acts addresses the Lord as the one who knows everyone's heart and asks him to show whom he has chosen.

column5: The Spirit gives the utterance that the disciples speak
column6: The commentary says the messenger receives and follows a recitation supplied by God. At Pentecost the disciples speak as the Spirit gives them utterance, extending divinely enabled speech from one prophet to a gathered community.

column5: Soldiers cast lots to divide Jesus' garment
column6: The commentary describes meysir as a game in which arrows assign portions of a slaughtered camel. John depicts soldiers using lots to divide Jesus' clothing, a concrete scene of chance allocation presented as an act of humiliation.

column5: The lot identifies Jonathan in a crisis
column6: The commentary distinguishes gambling for shares from an outcome assigned by divine measure. Saul's lot falls on Jonathan while the people seek the cause of a military crisis, showing lots used to identify responsibility rather than to win a game.
